Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah at the town of Beth-shemesh and brought him to Jerusalem. He broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.

He took the silver, gold, and vessels found in the LORD's house, along with the vessels of Obed-Edom, the treasures of the king's palace, the vessels of the king's palace, and the gold vessels, and returned to Samaria.
Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.
The rest of Amaziah's deeds, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
After Amaziah turned away from the fear of the LORD, his servants plotted against him in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, but they sent men after him to Lachish and killed him there.
His servants carried him on horses and buried him with his ancestors in the City of David.
All the people of Judah took his son Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king after his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after the king had rested with his ancestors.
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years. His mother's name was Jeconiah, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right before the Lord, just as David his ancestor had done.
He prayed before him in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of the LORD, and the LORD made all his ways prosper.
He went out and fought against the Philistines and broke down the walls of Gath, Gaza, and Ashdod.
His fame spread as far as the land of Egypt, because he waged war extensively.
Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate and the western gate, and reinforced their corners with iron bolts.

He built many towers in the villages that belonged to him and dug many cisterns for himself, because he had much livestock. He had farmers and laborers in the valleys and mountains, because he had extensive property.
Uzziah had mighty warriors who fought in battle.
They numbered thirty-two thousand six hundred.
He also had three hundred thousand people who lived in the wilderness. He had seven thousand five hundred men armed with swords who stood guard over the king every day.
His fame spread throughout all the provinces, until he had become exceedingly wealthy.
When he had become rich in possessions, his spirit became very proud, and he was unfaithful to the Lord his God. He entered the Lord’s temple to send up clouds of incense.
Uzziah the priest went in after him.
He said to him, “This position does not belong to you, O king, nor is it proper for you to offer incense on the altar.”

At that moment King Uzziah became angry with the priests and ordered them to be put out of the sanctuary. At that very moment, leprosy came out of the sanctuary and struck King Uzziah on his forehead, when he entered the Lord’s house to offer incense.
Uzziah the priest and all the priests turned toward him and saw that he was hurrying to leave, because he knew that the Lord had struck him.

King Uzziah continued to have leprosy until his death. While he had leprosy, he lived in the house of joy, because he had blasphemed against the Lord’s house. His son Jotham was in charge of the royal household and judged the people of the land.
The rest of Uzziah’s deeds, from first to last, are written in Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet.
Uzziah died and joined his ancestors. They buried him in the burial ground, but not in the tomb of the kings, because they said, “He has leprosy.” His son Jotham became king after him.
Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother’s name was Jerusha daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right before the Lord, just as his father Uzziah had done, except that he did not enter the Lord’s house. The people, however, continued to act corruptly, even until now.
He built the upper gate of the Lord's house, and he also did a great deal of building on the wall that had been completed.
He built towns in the land of Judah, and in the forest he built fortresses and towers.

He fought against the Ammonites and defeated them. That year the Ammonites gave him one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand kors of wheat, and ten thousand kors of barley. The Ammonites reckoned all this as tribute to present to him in the second and third years as well.
Jotham became strong because he set his ways right before the Lord God.
The rest of Jotham’s deeds, all his battles, and his ways are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
Jotham rested with his ancestors and was buried in the city of David. His son Ahaz became king after him.
Ahaz was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. He did not do what was right before the Lord his God, as his ancestor David had done.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel and also made altars for idols.
He sent up clouds of incense in the great valleys and made his son pass through fire, following the custom of the nations that the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.
He offered sacrifices and burned incense on the altars, on the high places, and under every beautiful tree.

The Lord God handed him over to the king of Edom, who inflicted a great slaughter on his people and took a large number of them captive. They came to Damascus. He was also handed over to the king of Israel, who inflicted a great slaughter on his people.

In one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed one hundred and twenty thousand men belonging to the king of Judah, all of them mighty warriors, because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors.
He killed Zichri, a mighty warrior of Ephraim, and Maaseiah the king’s son, Azrikam the palace steward, and Elkanah, who was second to the king.

The Israelites took captive two hundred thousand people from among their relatives, along with their sons and daughters. They also seized a great deal of plunder from them and brought the captives to Samaria.

There was a prophet of the Lord there named Oded. He went out to meet the army coming to Samaria and said, “Because the Lord, the God of their ancestors, was angry with the people of Judah, he handed them over to you. But you slaughtered them and showed them no mercy.
“Even now you are striving to make them your male and female slaves. Even now you know that you have committed this sin before the Lord your God.
“Now listen to me and send back the captives you took from your relatives, lest the Lord’s wrath rise against you.”
Men from among the leaders of Ephraim stood up: Azariah son of Johanan and Berechiah son of Mekriah.

They said to them, “Do not bring these captives here, so that we do not sin again before the Lord our God. Yet you are saying, ‘Let us add to our guilt and our sins,’ even though they are already very great.”
They sent all the captives back to Jerusalem.
At that time King Ahaz sent word to the king of Assyria to come to his aid.
Up to this time the Edomites had come and slaughtered people in Judah and taken captives from among them.

The Philistines came and encamped against the towns of the lowland and the southern towns of Judah. They captured the town of Beth-shemesh, the town of Aijalon, the town of Zaaroth, Shobi and its surrounding villages, Tekna and its surrounding villages, and Gerem and its surrounding villages.
For the Lord had brought Judah low because of the sins of Ahaz king of Judah, which had multiplied in Judah, and because he had been utterly unfaithful to the Lord his God.
Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came against him, encamped against him, and caused him great distress.

King Ahaz took the utensils that were in the house of the Lord, the utensils that had been in the houses of the former kings, and those in the houses of the wealthy, and gave them to the king of Assyria so that he would not harm him in his time of distress.
King Ahaz himself continued to act unfaithfully toward the Lord.

He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus and said to them, “You are my gods and my lords. You are the ones I worship, and to you I offer sacrifices.” He became a stumbling block to Judah, bringing himself and all the people of Judah into sin.

Ahaz gathered all the utensils that were in the house of the Lord and cut up the utensils that were in the house of the Lord. He shut the inner and outer doors of the house of the Lord and made altars for himself at every corner in Jerusalem.
In every town throughout Judah, he made altars for worshiping other gods.
The rest of the deeds of Ahaz and all his ways, from first to last, are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in Jerusalem, for they did not take him to the tombs of the kings of Judah. His son Hezekiah became king after him.
Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Ani, daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right before the Lord, just as David his ancestor had done.
In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and repaired them.
He brought in the priests and Levites and gathered them inside the courtyard of the sanctuary.
He said to them, “Listen to me, Levites. Now consecrate yourselves and consecrate the house of the Lord, the God of our ancestors, and remove your evil deeds from your thoughts.

Let us not do as our ancestors did. They did what was evil before the Lord our God and abandoned him. They turned their faces away from the Lord’s dwelling, turned their backs, and showed them to him.
They also shut the lattice doors, extinguished the lamps, and did not offer incense on the altar of the God of Israel.
The Lord’s anger came upon Judah and Jerusalem, and he handed them over to a curse, desolation, and the sword, as you see with your own eyes.

Look, our ancestors have fallen by the sword, and our wives, sons, and daughters are in captivity. Even now, because we have strayed from following the Lord our God and have abandoned the covenant he gave our ancestors, he too has abandoned us.”
King Hezekiah rose early, gathered the elders of Jerusalem, and entered the house of the Lord.

They brought him seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats to make atonement for the kingdom, for Judah, and for the sanctuary. He told the sons of Aaron the priest to offer burnt offerings on the altar of the Lord.
They were to slaughter the bulls, and the priests were to receive their blood and sprinkle it on the horns of the altar.
They were to bring the male goats before the Lord, before the king, and before the people of Israel, and lay their hands on them.

The priests were to slaughter them, splash their blood on the horns of the altar, and make atonement for all Israel, because the king had commanded that burnt offerings and sacrifices be brought for all Israel.

He stationed the Levites in the house of the Lord with songs of praise to the sound of lyres, with the songs of David and the songs of Gad, King David’s prophet, and of Nathan, King David’s prophet. For David used to sing praises to the Lord his God according to the words spoken by the prophets.
The Levites stood singing David’s songs of praise, while the priests sounded curved and straight horns.

Hezekiah ordered that burnt offerings be offered on the altar. When the offering of the burnt offerings began, Hezekiah began to sing the praises of the Lord according to the words spoken by David, king of Israel.
All the people of Israel were bowing down, singing praises, and sounding curved and straight horns until they finished offering the burnt offerings.
When they finished offering the burnt offerings, the king knelt on his knees, and everyone who was with him fell down and worshiped.
King Hezekiah and the officials told the Levites to praise the Lord with the words of David and Asaph the prophet. They praised him with great joy, then fell down and worshiped.

Hezekiah spoke and said, “Now that you have drawn near to the way of the Lord, come forward and bring me sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the Lord.” The people brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and they brought whatever their hearts desired.
The number of burnt offerings the people brought was seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs. All these were for a burnt offering to the Lord.
The animals consecrated were six hundred bulls and three thousand sheep.

But the priests were few and could not attend to all the burnt offerings. Their fellow Levites helped them until all the work was finished. After this, the priests consecrated themselves, for the Levites were more humble in heart about consecrating themselves than the priests were.
There were also abundant burnt offerings, as well as the fat of the fellowship offerings and the lambs for the burnt offerings. Thus the work of the house of the Lord was completed.
Hezekiah and all the people of Israel rejoiced that the work of the house was completed, for the matter had come about suddenly.

Hezekiah sent word to all Israel and the house of Judah. He also wrote letters to the house of Ephraim and the house of Manasseh, telling them to come to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem to celebrate a festival for the mighty Lord, the God of Israel.
The king, his officials, and all the people of Israel who were in Jerusalem decided to celebrate a festival for the Lord, the God of Israel, in the second month.
For they could not celebrate it at that time, because the priests had not consecrated themselves and the teachers of the people had not gathered in Jerusalem.
The proposal pleased the king and all the people of Israel.

They arose and confirmed the decision to celebrate it, and they sent a proclamation throughout Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, that people should come and celebrate the festival for the LORD, the God of Israel, in Jerusalem, because their wealth was very great.

The couriers went throughout Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his officials, at the king’s command, saying, “People of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and he will restore the remnant of you who have survived from the hands of the king of Assyria.
Do not be like your ancestors and your brothers, who were unfaithful to the LORD, the God of our ancestors, so that he handed them over to a curse, as you yourselves see.
And now, do not be stubborn like your ancestors. Enter the sanctuary that has been consecrated forever, and serve the LORD your God, so that he may turn his fierce anger away from you.

For he has revealed himself to you, to your brothers, and to your children. He will grant you compassion in the eyes of your captors and bring you back to this land, because the LORD your God is gracious and compassionate. He will not turn his face away from you when you turn to him.”
The couriers of King Hezekiah went from town to town through the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, as far as Zebulun, but people laughed at them and treated them with contempt.
Wicked men were in the tribe of Asher, the tribe of Ephraim, the tribe of Manasseh, and the tribe of Zebulun. The rest of these tribes were humbled in their hearts and came to Jerusalem.
Together with the tribe of Judah, the hand of the LORD was upon them, giving them one heart to carry out the command of the king and his officials, according to the word of the LORD.
Many people gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread in the second month—a very great crowd.
They arose and tore down the altars in Jerusalem. They also tore down all the high places of the idols and threw them into the Kidron Valley.
They celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth, for seven days [?], in the second month. The priests and Levites consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings to the house of the LORD.
They stood in their appointed places, as was fitting, according to what is written in the law of Moses, the prophet of the LORD. The priests received the blood from the hands of the Levites.

For there were many among the people of Israel who had not consecrated themselves. The Levites took charge of slaughtering the lambs and watched over everyone who was clean enough to be consecrated to the LORD.

For there were many among the people of Israel from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun—these four tribes—who had not purified themselves, yet ate the Passover contrary to the law. For Hezekiah prayed for them and said to them, “May the good God make atonement for all the people of Israel.”
For our hearts have been prepared to pray to the Lord, the God of our ancestors, but the sanctuary had not been purified by us.
The Lord listened to Hezekiah's voice and healed the people.

The Israelites who were present in Jerusalem celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy. Every day they praised the LORD: the Levites with praises from their mouths, and the priests with praises.

Hezekiah spoke with all the Levites who were singing good praises before the LORD. The men ate for seven days, offering sacrifices of well-being to the LORD and giving thanks to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
All the people of Israel stayed to celebrate another seven days—seven days of joy.

For Hezekiah king of Judah set aside and gave the people seven thousand animals, both large and small livestock. He also set aside and gave the people of Israel a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep, and many priests consecrated themselves.

All the people of Judah rejoiced, along with the priests and Levites, all the people who had come from the people of Israel, and the resident foreigners who had come from the land of Israel and those who lived in Judah.
There was great joy in Jerusalem, because since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel, there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem.
The priests and Levites arose and blessed the people of Israel. The LORD heard their voice, and their prayer entered his holy dwelling in heaven.

When all these things were finished, all the Israelites who were present went out to the towns of Judah. They smashed the sacred pillars, smashed the [?], tore down the altars, and tore down the high places in Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Then Israel returned, and they all came to their own inherited property and entered their towns in peace.

Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and Levites to their duties, each man according to his service, for the priests and Levites, for burnt offerings and offerings of well-being, to minister, give thanks, and offer praise at the gate of the LORD.

The king gave from his own possessions bulls for the morning and evening burnt offerings, and burnt offerings for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the festivals. He instructed the people according to what is written in the law of the LORD.
He told the Israelites living in Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and Levites, because this would strengthen them in the law of the LORD.

When the command spread throughout Israel, they brought the firstfruits of grain, wine, and oil, and offerings from their livestock and the produce of the fields. They also brought tithes in abundance.

The people of Israel and Judah who lived in the towns of Judah also brought a tenth. They brought tithes and offered them to the Lord their God. They brought firstfruits upon firstfruits of grain, wine, and oil, and offerings from their livestock and the produce of the fields. They brought a tenth and dedicated it to the Lord their God.
In the third month there was a very great abundance of firstfruits, and in the seventh month

Hezekiah took it and distributed it to the priests and Levites. Hezekiah and the leaders saw that the firstfruits belonging to the priests were very abundant, and they blessed the Lord and prayed for Israel.
Hezekiah prayed for the priests and Levites concerning the abundant firstfruits.

He spoke to Azariah, the chief priest from the family of Zadok, and said to him, “You are permitted to eat these firstfruits, because they have come into the Lord’s house. Eat your fill, and give what remains to the poor and needy, because the Lord has blessed his people and given them this abundance.” And they gave what remained to all the people of Israel.
Hezekiah ordered that chambers be prepared in the house of the Lord, and they prepared them.
They faithfully brought in the firstfruits, the tithes, and the sacred offerings. Conaniah the Levite was in charge of them, with his brother Shimei as his deputy.

Jehiel, Uzziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabar, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, Benaiah, and his brother Shemaiah—all these served as overseers under Conaniah, by the authority of King Hezekiah and Azariah, the supervisor of the Lord’s house.
Kore son of Imnah, a Levite and keeper of the eastern gate, was in charge of the offerings to the Lord and the most holy things.
Eden, Benjamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah were accountable to him in the towns of the priests, faithfully giving their brothers their portions, to the older and younger alike.

This was apart from what was due to males three years old and upward—to everyone who entered the Lord’s house for his daily assignment, to perform their service according to their duties and divisions.
Oil and wine were given to the priests and Levites according to their ancestral households, from twenty years old and upward, according to their duties and divisions.
Oil was given to their [?], their wives, their sons, their daughters, and all the people of Israel who faithfully consecrated themselves, because they were holy.

The descendants of Aaron the priest—their bodies were holy, and they did not approach women. Men whose names were known went around every town to give the allotted portion to every male among the priests and to all the families of the Levites.
Hezekiah did this throughout Judah. He did what was good and right and lived faithfully before the Lord.
In all the work he began to do in the Lord’s house, and in the law and the commandment, he sought his God with all his heart. He acted and prospered.

After these events and this faithfulness that Hezekiah had shown, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and encamped against Judah, against its strong fortresses. He said to their inhabitants, “Accept my pledge and come over to me.”
Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib king of Assyria and his armies had come to wage war against Jerusalem.
He took counsel with his officials and warriors about blocking the water of the springs outside the city, and his officials helped him.

A very large number of the people of Israel gathered and blocked all the springs and the great streams within the land. For they said, “Why should the king of Assyria come and they find abundant water,
and grow strong and build a wall opposite another wall and fill in the ditch that David made?” Hezekiah made many weapons, shields, and spears.
He appointed fighting men over the people, one over every ten. He gathered them to him in the town square, spoke with them all, and said to them,
“Be brave and strong. Do not be afraid or tremble before the king of Assyria or before the armies that have come with him, for the one with us is greater than the one with him.
With him is human strength, but with us is the Lord our God, to help us and fight our battles.” The people took heart at the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.

After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh, who came to Jerusalem with his servants. Sennacherib himself was encamped against Lachish with his officials. The Rabshakeh addressed all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem and said to them,
“This is what Sennacherib king of Assyria says: On whom are you relying, that you remain under siege in Jerusalem?
Hezekiah is misleading you, handing you over to die of hunger and thirst. He misleads you and tells you, ‘The Lord our God will rescue us from the hands of the king of Assyria.’
Where is this Hezekiah who removed the high places and altars and told the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before one altar and burn incense on it’?
Surely you know what I and my ancestors have done to all the peoples in the cities. The gods of these peoples could not rescue their cities from my hands.
Who among all the gods of these nations that my ancestors destroyed was able to rescue their cities from my hands, that the Lord should be able to rescue you from my hands?

Even now, do not let Hezekiah mislead you or make you trust in this. Do not believe him, because your God cannot rescue you from my hands. All the nations and kingdoms were unable to rescue their cities from my hands or from the hands of my ancestors, and your God cannot rescue you from my hands either.
His servants spoke these things against the Lord God and against Hezekiah his servant.

He also wrote letters insulting the Lord, the God of Israel, and telling the people of Israel, “The gods of these cities could not rescue their cities from my hands. Neither can Hezekiah’s God rescue his city from my hands.”
They called out loudly in the language of Judah to the people sitting on the wall of Jerusalem, to frighten and terrify them so that they could capture the city wall.
They spoke against the gods of the peoples of the earth and also against the God who rules in Jerusalem, who would repay them for the deeds of their hands.
Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz prayed about this, and the Lord heard their prayer.

The Lord sent an angel from his presence and destroyed all the mighty warriors, kings, and rulers who were in the camp of the king of Assyria. The king of Assyria returned to his city in shame. He entered the temple of his gods, and there his sons, who had come from his own body, killed him with the sword.
The Lord rescued Hezekiah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hands of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hands of all their neighbors.
Many of the Israelites brought offerings to the Lord in Jerusalem and gave gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah. He was exalted above all the nations. And after these things,
in those days Hezekiah became sick to the point of death. He prayed before the Lord and said, “You have done many mighty deeds for me,
and you have not repaid me according to the work of my hands.” Hezekiah became sick because his heart had grown proud, and wrath came upon him, upon Judah, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
Hezekiah became sick in the pride of his heart, he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. But the Lord’s wrath did not come upon them during Hezekiah’s lifetime.
Hezekiah had very great wealth and honor. He made treasuries for himself for silver, gold, precious stones, spices, pearls, and all kinds of desirable objects.
And storehouses for the produce of grain, wine, and oil, and stalls for all the livestock.
He also made villages for livestock, sheep, cattle, and animals, because the Lord had given him very great possessions.
Hezekiah himself blocked the water outlet of the upper spring and diverted the water westward to the City of David. Hezekiah prospered in everything he did.
And he followed the law of the LORD as it had been given to him in the land, and he knew everything that was in his heart.
The rest of Hezekiah’s deeds, his acts of kindness, and his good ways are written in the prophecy of Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, and also in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

Hezekiah rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in the City of David. All the people of Judah paid him great honor at his death and returned to Jerusalem. His son Manasseh became king after him.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-five years.
He did what was evil before the LORD, following the practices of the nations whom the LORD had uprooted before the Israelites.
He rebuilt the altars that his father Hezekiah had torn down, set up high places for idols, made leopards, and worshiped them and all the heavenly armies.
In the two courtyards of the LORD’s house.

He also made his son pass through the fire in the great valley. He practiced illusion, divination, and sorcery, and consulted Chaldean diviners and mediums. He did much evil before the Lord, provoking him to anger.

He placed the four-faced image he had made in the house of the Lord, about which the Lord had said to David and his son Solomon, “In this house in Jerusalem, which I have chosen for myself from all the tribes of Israel, I will establish my presence forever.

I will never again remove Israel from this land that I gave to their ancestors, provided that they are careful to do everything I commanded them, keeping the whole law, its statutes, and its judgments, which my servant Moses commanded them.”
Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, making them do evil deeds like the nations the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they would not listen.
The Lord brought against them the army commanders of the king of Assyria. They captured Manasseh alive, bound him with chains, and took him to Babylon.
When he was in distress, he prayed before the LORD his God and was greatly afraid before the LORD, the God of his ancestors.
He prayed before the Lord, who listened to him, accepted his prayer, and brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the Lord is God.

After these things, he built an outer wall for the City of David, west of the Gihon River and as far as the entrance to the Fishermen’s Gate. He surrounded all Jerusalem with an outer wall and made it very high. He stationed army commanders in all the elevated towns of Judah.

He removed the foreign gods and the carved images that were in the house of the Lord, along with all the high places he had built on the mountain of the Lord’s house and in Jerusalem, and threw them outside the city.
He built an altar to the Lord and offered burnt offerings, peace offerings, and thanksgiving offerings. He told Judah to serve the Lord, the God of Israel.
“Do not again celebrate a festival or offer other sacrifices on the high places, but only before the LORD your God.”

The rest of the deeds of Manasseh, his prayer before his God, and the words of the prophets who prophesied concerning him in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, are written in the accounts of the kings of Israel and Judah.

His prayer, how his plea was heard, all his sins and wrongdoing, the places where he built altars and appointed pagan priests, and the shrines he made for idols are written in the accounts of Hanan the prophet.
Manasseh rested with his ancestors, and they buried him at his house, in the garden of Gaza. His son Amon reigned in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for two years.
He did what was evil before the Lord, just as his father Manasseh had done. Amon sacrificed to and worshiped all the images and idols that his father Manasseh had made.
He did not tremble before the Lord his God, although Manasseh himself had trembled before the Lord his God. Instead, Amon sinned more and more.
His servants conspired against him and killed him in his house.
The people of the land killed everyone who had plotted against King Amon, and the people of the land made his son Josiah king after him.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years.
He did what was right before the Lord and walked in the ways of his ancestor David, without turning aside from them to the right or to the left.

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still a young boy, he began to pray to the God of his ancestor David. In the twelfth year, he began to cleanse Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. He began to uproot the high places, idols, leopards, shrines, necklaces, and bells.
He broke and crushed all the trees that had been prepared for idols, and scattered their ashes among the graves of the people who had sacrificed to them.
He dug the bones of the pagan priests who had served them out of their graves, brought them out, and burned them. He cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.
and the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali, in their streets all around.
He tore down the altars and broke the images, crushing them into dust and scattering them throughout the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, he cleansed the land of Israel and his house. He sent Shaphan son of Azaliah and Maaseiah, the city scribe, and told them, “Go and repair the house of the Lord your God.”

They came to Hilkiah the high priest and delivered the money that had been brought into the house of the Lord, which the Levite gatekeepers had collected from Manasseh and Ephraim, from all the people of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
They handed it over to the workers who supervised the house of the Lord. These gave the money to the workers in the Lord’s house for repairing and restoring the building.
They gave it to the carpenters, the builders, and those buying good stone blocks and timber to repair and restore the house that the kings of Judah had closed up.

The men faithfully carried out the work on the sanctuary. Their supervisors were Nahath and Obadiah, descendants of Merari, and Zechariah and Shallum, descendants of Kohath, along with the singers and the Levites who offered praise with musical instruments.
And all those who performed work, for the tasks; and from the Levites, scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.
As they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the house of the Lord, Hilkiah the priest found the book of the Lord’s law that had been given through Moses.
Hilkiah the priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord.” Hilkiah the priest gave the book to Shaphan.
Shaphan the scribe told the king everything Hilkiah had said to him. He also reported to him, saying, “Your servants are doing everything you entrusted to them.
They are bringing out the money for repairing the house of the Lord and giving an account of it to the overseers and the workers.”
Shaphan the scribe also informed the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has given me a book.” And Shaphan read from it before the king.
When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes.
The king gave orders to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asa, the king’s chief steward, saying to them:

“Go and pray before the Lord for me, for the people of Israel, and for Judah concerning the words of this book that has been found. For great is the Lord’s anger that is coming upon us, because our ancestors did not obey the words of the Lord by doing everything written concerning us in this book.”

Hilkiah and all those whom the king had sent went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Hadhas, the keeper of the garments. She lived in Jerusalem, in the school. They spoke with her according to the king’s command.
She said to them, “This is what the Lord of lords of Israel says: Tell the man who sent you to me,
This is what the Lord says: Look, I am bringing disaster on this place and its inhabitants—all the curses written in the book that was read before the king of Judah.
Because they abandoned me, worshiped other gods, and angered me with the work of their hands, my wrath will come upon this place and will not be extinguished.
To the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, say this: This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says concerning the words you heard:

Because your heart was broken and you trembled before the Lord when you heard these words about what I am bringing upon this place and its inhabitants, and because you humbled yourself before me, tore your clothes, and wept before me, I too have heard, says the Lord.

Therefore I will gather you to your ancestors, and you will be gathered to your tomb in peace. Your eyes will not see all the disaster that I am bringing upon this place and its inhabitants. They brought the answer back to the king.
The king sent word, and all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem gathered before him.

The king went up to the house of the Lord, together with all the people of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests, the Levites, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. He read before them all the words of the book of this covenant that had been found in the house of the Lord.

The king stood in his place and swore an oath before the Lord to follow the Lord, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, laws, and testimonies with all his heart and all his soul, carrying out the words of this covenant written in this book.
He brought forward everyone who was found in Jerusalem and Benjamin, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem entered into the covenant of the Lord, the God of their ancestors.

Josiah removed the detestable practices that the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites. All the people who were found in Israel acted and served the Lord their God, and they did not turn away from following the God of their ancestors.
Josiah celebrated a festival to the Lord in Jerusalem. He celebrated the festival on the fourteenth day of the first month.
He appointed the priests to their duties and assigned them to the work of the house of the Lord.

He said to the Levites who stood among all the Israelites, “Consecrate yourselves to the Lord, and put the holy ark in the house that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built. You no longer have to carry it on your shoulders. From now on, serve the Lord your God and his people Israel.”
“Prepare your hearts and the hearts of your ancestors, according to what David king of Israel wrote and what his son Solomon wrote.”
“Stand in the sanctuary according to the divisions of your ancestral houses and those of your fellow countrymen, according to the divisions of the ancestral houses of the Levites.”
“Slaughter the Passover sacrifice, consecrate yourselves, and prepare the hearts of your brothers so that they may act according to what the Lord said to your brothers.”

Josiah set aside flocks, lambs, and young goats for the people—all these for the Passover, for everyone who was present—thirty thousand in number, together with three thousand cattle. These came from the king’s property.

His officials also set aside offerings for the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Nahael, the officials of the house of the Lord, set aside offerings for the priests and gave two thousand six hundred for the Passover, together with three hundred sheep.
Conaniah, Shemaiah his brother’s son, Hashabiah, and Jedaiel set aside five thousand sheep and five hundred cattle for the Levites for the Passover.
The service was put in order, and the priests stood at their posts, and the Levites at theirs.
They slaughtered the Passover sacrifice according to the king’s command. The priests sprinkled some of the blood, while the Levites skinned the animals.
They gave the burnt offerings to the divisions of the people’s ancestral houses to offer to the Lord, as it is written in the law of Moses. This is how they made offerings every morning.
They cooked the Passover sacrifice over the fire as required, and they cooked its sacred offerings over the fire in pots, cauldrons, and kettles. All the people hurried.

After these things, the priests prepared their own portions, because the priests were Aaron’s descendants and were offering up burnt offerings and fat up to the Levites [?]. The Levites prepared portions for themselves and for the priests, Aaron’s descendants.

The sons of Asaph served at their stations according to the command of David and [?] Heman and Jeduthun, the king’s seers. The gatekeepers were at every gate and did not have to stop any of their work, because their brothers had prepared portions for them.
All the service of the Lord was prepared that day for celebrating the Passover, and they offered burnt offerings on the altar of the Lord according to the command of King Josiah.
The Israelites who were present celebrated the Passover at that time, and the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

No festival like that one had been celebrated in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had celebrated a Passover like the one celebrated by Josiah, the priests, the Levites, and all Judah and Israel who were present in Jerusalem.
This festival was celebrated in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign.
After all these things, when Josiah had put the affairs of the temple in order, Pharaoh the Lame, king of Egypt, went up to fight against Mabbug on the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him.

He sent messengers to him and said, “What do I have to do with you, king of Judah? I am not coming against you today, king of Judah, for I am not coming to fight against you. The LORD has told you to fear me. Keep away from me, so that God, who is with me, does not destroy you.”

Josiah did not turn away from him, because he was going to fight and wage war. He did not listen to the words of Pharaoh the Lame, and Josiah did not know that this had come from the LORD. He went out to fight him in the plain of Megiddo.
Pharaoh the Lame struck Josiah with two arrows. The king said to his servants, “Take me away, because I am mortally wounded.”

His servants took him out of the chariot, put him in his royal carriage, and brought him to Jerusalem. He died, and they buried him in the tomb of his ancestors. All the house of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem observed mourning for Josiah.

Jeremiah lamented over Josiah and said, “All you righteous men and women, weep for Josiah in your lamentations.” He established these as an ordinance for Israel to this day, and they are written in the Book of Lamentations.
And the rest of Josiah’s deeds and his acts of kindness, in accordance with what is written in the LORD’s law.
His acts, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in Jerusalem in place of his father.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months.
The king of Egypt removed him.

He appointed his brother Eliakim over the house of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Pharaoh the Lame took his brother Jehoahaz away and brought him to Egypt, where he died.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. He did what was evil before the LORD his God.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar brought some of all the furnishings of the house to Babylon and placed them in his temple in Babylon.
The rest of Jehoiakim’s deeds and the detestable things he did are written in the books of the kings of Israel and Judah. His son Jehoiachin became king after him.
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for one hundred days. He did what was evil before the LORD.

At the end of the year, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon sent against him and brought him to Babylon, together with the precious vessels that were in the LORD’s house. He appointed his uncle Zedekiah as king over Judah and Jerusalem.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years.
He did what was evil before the LORD his God. He did not fear Jeremiah the prophet, who prophesied as one speaking from the mouth of the LORD.
He also rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, to whom he had sworn an oath in the LORD’s name. He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart, and would not pray before the LORD, the God of Israel.
The elders of the priests, the Levites, and the people also acted more and more deceitfully, following all the practices of the nations. They defiled the LORD’s holy house in Jerusalem.
The LORD, the God of their ancestors, sent messages to them through his messengers, early and late, because he had compassion on his people and on the flock he had chosen.
But they laughed at the LORD’s messengers, despised their words, and mocked his prophets, until the LORD’s anger rose against his people to the point that there was no remedy for them.

He brought the king of the Chaldeans against them, and he killed their young men with the sword in their sanctuary. He spared neither youths nor young women, neither the elderly nor even nursing infants. He handed them all over to him.
He carried everything away to Babylon: all the vessels of the LORD’s house, large and small, the treasure of the LORD’s house, and the treasure of the king and his officials.
He burned the LORD’s house, tore down Jerusalem’s walls, burned all its palaces with fire, and destroyed every precious vessel.
He took those who had escaped the sword into captivity in Babylon. They became servants to him and his sons, until he handed the kingdom over to the Persians.
This fulfilled the LORD’s word spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, until the land rested during its Sabbaths, throughout all the days it lay desolate, completing seventy years.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the LORD’s word through the mouth of Jeremiah the prophet, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia. He issued a proclamation throughout his kingdom, and his name was also declared in writing.

This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: “The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who among you belongs to all the people whom the LORD his God favors? Let him go up and come to me.”
